newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to open regional offices on environment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to open regional offices on environment.

text.p: The United States will open offices in 12 countries to tackle regional environmental problems as part of a new "green" slant to its foreign policy, the State Department said on Tuesday.
The announcement came in the department's first annual report on world ecological problems which picked out five key issues that would be the focus of "environmental diplomacy."
"Regional environmental hubs" will be opened this year in U.S. embassies in Costa Rica, Uzbekistan, Ethiopia, Nepal, Jordan and Thailand, the report said.
Six more hubs in unspecified capitals will be opened next year to help neighbouring countries tackle problems specific to their regions, said the report, issued on Earth Day.

Former secretary of state Warren Christopher decided last year to upgrade environmental issues on the State Department's agenda, and Vice President Al Gore said the publication of the report marked a "turning point in U.S. foreign policy."
Gore and current Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in separate introductions to the 32-page report that environmental problems were now considered an integral part of U.S. national security.
"All the missiles and artillery in our arsenal will not be able to protect our people from rising sea levels, poisoned air, or foods laced with pesticides," Gore said.

Albright said Soviet-era environmental disasters were impeding reform in Russia and central Europe, while population growth and competition for scarce resources were fuelling "conflict and misery" in Central Africa.
She said the administration was focusing on five global problems -- climate change, toxic chemicals, species extinction, deforestation and marine degradation.

At a news conference, Albright said that at a December conference on climate change in Kyoto, Japan, the United States would press for "clear, common and enforceable targets for greenhouse gas emissions." She did not say what the targets would be.
She also said Washington would seek to negotiate a global agreement to ban or minimise the release of 12 of the most hazardous and persistent toxic chemicals.
Unlike the State Department's annual human rights report, the environmental report avoided targeting specific countries and said only a cooperative approach would work.
The World Bank needed to factor environmental implications into its lending decisions, and the United Nations should be reformed to coordinate international action, it said.
Among statistics cited in the report were:
-- Seventy percent of the world's marine fish stocks are "fully to over-exploited";
-- The people of the world annually release 23 billion tons of carbon dioxide into the air, raising the earth's temperature;
-- An estimated 70 species of living things are lost forever every day.
